query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (around 0.5 atomic percent) of tungsten (W) to a CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote a beneficial lattice distortion that drives in situ formation of a stable, nanocrystalline, reactive tribolayer during sliding. This self‐adjusting surface structure is expected to maintain low friction and low wear rates across the entire temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline, single‐phase CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix that shows acceptable friction and wear at room temperature but experiences degradation (from softening and oxidation) at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying with tungsten (approximately 0.5 at.%), introduced as a dopant during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under controlled normal loads and in air, with temperatures varied from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and refines the microstructure, enhancing the alloy’s reactivity with environmental oxygen to form a continuous, nanocrystalline glaze layer (a reactive oxide/tribolayer) which acts as a protective, self-lubricating interface.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the introduced W atoms intensify lattice strain, promoting multiple deformation pathways at the surface. At elevated temperatures, frictional heating and exposure to oxygen trigger rapid formation of a nanocrystalline oxide tribolayer that suppresses adhesive/oxidative wear. At lower temperatures, the modified subsurface microstructure accommodates plastic deformation effectively, keeping friction low.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the W-doped variant will exhibit a lower, more stable coefficient of friction as well as reduced wear rates over a broad temperature range, thanks to the formation of an in situ protective nanolayer that adapts to temperature-induced changes.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition, which tends to lose wear and friction performance at high temperatures due to surface softening and less effective oxide layer formation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under moderate to high contact stresses and in ambient air. Its benefits may be limited if operating conditions exceed the tested range (e.g., extremely high loads or aggressive environments) or if processing parameters do not yield the desired microstructural refinement.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines findings that nanohierarchical architectures can improve wear resistance (e.g., PMC10241162 evidence) with reports that small W additions in related HEA systems (PMC8470387 evidence) dramatically enhance high-temperature wear behavior. Extension from systems containing Al (or related components) to a pure CoCrFeNi system is plausible but remains to be verified, and the optimal W concentration and processing route may require fine-tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the standard CoCrFeNi alloy and another of CoCrFeNi alloy doped with approximately 0.5 at.% W. Process both sets under identical conditions. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding wear tests at room temperature, mid-range temperature (e.g., ~400 °C) and at 800 °C under identical load and sliding speed. Post-test, characterize the worn surfaces using SEM/TEM and XRD to assess tribolayer formation and phase stability.
measurements: Time-resolved coefficient of friction during sliding tests
Wear rate calculated from volume loss (mm³/N·m)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure (SEM, TEM) to identify formation and continuity of the nanocrystalline tribolayer
XRD phase analysis to evaluate any phase changes due to W addition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W-doped CoCrFeNi alloy does not consistently exhibit a significantly lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the temperature range (or if no evidence for a beneficial, continuous tribolayer is observed) compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 shows the influence of the W powder addition on the high temperature friction and wear properties of the AlCoCrFeNiWx coatings on H13 steel. The H13 steel exhibits a maximum friction coefficient and wear loss after 800 °C/60 min high temperature friction and wear treatment. Compared to the H13 steel, all HEA coatings exhibit smaller friction coefficient and wear loss. A minimum friction coefficient and wear loss (only 12% of H13 steel wear loss) occurs in the AlCoCrFeNiWx with the addition of 0.5 at.% W. Consequently, a great improvement in the high temperature friction and wear resistance is achieved by the addition of the W powder and is likely due to the lattice distortion becoming more remarkable; the unmelted W-rich particles also improve the wear resistance as the hard phase. The addition of 0.5 at.% W powder in AlCoCrFeNi HEA system can improve its high temperature friction and wear resistance. These results are also supported by wear scars height and width of samples. The distinct differences are observed with regard to three-dimensional morphologies, as shown in Figure 7.
